title: NASA's New Mars Helicopters Look Like Sci-Fi Come to Life!
summary: Imagine three helicopters flying over Mars, beaming green and red lasers at the ground. That's what NASA's new SkyFall mission will look like! The space agency just released an artist's picture of these awesome machines in action. SkyFall is set to launch in late 2028 aboard a spacecraft called Space Reactor-1 Freedom. The helicopters will use a "daring mid-air deployment"—that means they'll be dropped from the sky while still in the air! Their job is to map what's under the Martian surface. They have special instruments to see underground ice, take pictures, and check temperatures. In the new image, green waves show radar scanning below the dirt, and red beams show near-infrared cameras looking at rocks and soil. The helicopters have flexible antennas covered in polyester and Vectran, a super-strong fiber also used in Mars rover airbags. These antennas let the helicopters fly close to the ground without breaking. "The only way to detect shallow subsurface ice remotely is to fly close to the ground," says Adrian Tang, the radar scientist. Flying low and slow, they can spot where dry soil turns to ice. Unlike the first Mars helicopter, Ingenuity, which needed the Perseverance rover to send messages, SkyFall can talk directly to spacecraft orbiting Mars. Now we just have to wait to see what secrets are hiding under the red dirt!
why_it_matters: Learning to find water on Mars helps scientists plan for future space explorers, and you could be one of them someday.

background_read: NASA (the U.S. space agency) has already flown a small helicopter on Mars called Ingenuity; it was the first aircraft to fly on another planet.
Mars is a cold, dry planet, but scientists believe frozen water is hidden under parts of its surface.
Knowing where that ice is could help future astronauts find water and study Mars's past.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA and radar scientist Adrian Tang are behind the SkyFall mission
WHAT: Three helicopters dropped mid-air will use green radar and red near-infrared cameras to map what is under Mars's surface
WHERE: On Mars, scanning below the Martian surface
WHY: To detect shallow underground ice and learn what is hiding under the red dirt

perspectives.description: NASA fans and space scientists are excited because SkyFall can scan under Mars's surface without needing a rover nearby.
Some engineers may worry because dropping helicopters mid-air and flying low with antennas is risky and hard to pull off.
Scientists like Adrian Tang see this as one of the only ways to detect shallow subsurface ice remotely, so they accept the challenge.
